classification.difficultyReason: Read centre and radius from standard circle equations, sketch the translated circles and substitute an axis coordinate to obtain exact intercepts. These are routine linked representations and algebraic steps.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b use the origin form; parts c and d use the translated-centre form. The teacher answer additionally labels the axis intercepts, found by setting the other coordinate to zero.
questions.methodNote: The inspected original teaching gives x²+y²=r² for an origin-centred circle and (x−h)²+(y−k)²=r² for centre (h,k), and sketches a circle from its centre and radius.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify centres and radii from standard circle equations, then translate these into sketches and determine axis intercepts for the translated circle.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute a given centre and radius into the standard circle equation, including a surd radius.

questions.mappingNote: The inspected Chapter 11 circle summary gives the standard equation for centre $(h,k)$ and radius $r$, directly supporting both parts.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the centre coordinates and radius into $(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2$, then simplify.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute a given centre and radius into the standard circle equation, including a surd radius.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete the square in both variables, then interpret the standard circle equation.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts assess conversion to the standard circle equation and interpretation of its centre and radius, so circle-equation-general is primary and complete-square-form is secondary.
questions.methodNote: The supplied Chapter 11 page 3 establishes the standard circle equation and identifies its centre and radius. Completing-the-square demonstrations are not supplied; the authored working completes each variable's square by adding equal quantities to both sides.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Complete the square in both variables, then interpret the standard circle equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch reciprocal graphs with changes of sign and horizontal or vertical translations, identifying asymptotes and intercepts.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess hyperbola transformations. Neither supplied circle teaching nor the line/curve intersection introduction establishes the required transformation method.
questions.methodNote: Provisional solutions use reciprocal-graph translations, asymptotes and algebraic intercept calculations. The supplied external pages do not demonstrate this method.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch reciprocal graphs with changes of sign and horizontal or vertical translations, identifying asymptotes and intercepts.

classification.difficultyReason: Equate a line and a quadratic or reciprocal expression, solve the resulting quadratic by factorisation, and find both intersection coordinates.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b equate a line with a parabola; parts c and d equate a line with a rectangular hyperbola. Factorisation finds the x-values, followed by substitution into the line for each y-value.
questions.methodNote: The inspected Chapter 11 introduction identifies intersections of lines with parabolas and rectangular hyperbolas and directs students to solve simultaneous equations algebraically.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Equate a line and a quadratic or reciprocal expression, solve the resulting quadratic by factorisation, and find both intersection coordinates.

classification.difficultyReason: Solve simultaneous line and circle equations by substitution, including a quadratic with an exact surd coefficient.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly assesses intersections of a line and a circle. The translated-circle and other retrieval candidates are different original tasks and are not reused.
questions.methodNote: Solve the simultaneous equations by substituting the line equation into the circle equation, solve the resulting quadratic exactly, then find the corresponding second coordinates. The inspected introduction identifies simultaneous equations as the method for finding line–circle intersections; the circle teaching establishes the circle equations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Solve simultaneous line and circle equations by substitution, including a quadratic with an exact surd coefficient.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute a linear expression into a circle equation, solve the resulting quadratic and find both coordinate pairs.

questions.mappingNote: Both supplied equations define the line–circle intersection task directly assessed by intersection-line-curve.
questions.methodNote: The inspected original Chapter 11 introduction identifies intersections of a line and a circle as simultaneous-equation problems. Rearrange the line, substitute into the circle, solve the quadratic and substitute back for each ordinate.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute a linear expression into a circle equation, solve the resulting quadratic and find both coordinate pairs.

classification.difficultyReason: Rearrange the line equation, substitute into the parabola equation, factorise and calculate both intersection coordinates.

questions.mappingNote: Both intersection coordinates are required, so intersection-line-curve is the directly assessed skill. The supplied introduction establishes the algebraic approach but does not show its worked substitution sequence.
questions.methodNote: The inspected Chapter 11 introduction teaches finding line–parabola intersections by solving simultaneous equations. The solution substitutes the rearranged line equation and factorises the resulting quadratic.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rearrange the line equation, substitute into the parabola equation, factorise and calculate both intersection coordinates.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch linear, circular and hyperbolic boundaries, distinguish strict inequalities and select the required regions.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–b assess linear boundary and region selection; c–e extend circle equations to regions; f combines a translated reciprocal graph with region selection. No supplied reuse candidate has this complete task.
questions.methodNote: The inspected external circle teaching establishes centre-radius form. The required inequality-region and translated-hyperbola demonstrations were not supplied; compatibility with those taught procedures remains unresolved.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch linear, circular and hyperbolic boundaries, distinguish strict inequalities and select the required regions.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine several inclusive linear inequalities and calculate the vertices of their common region.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts directly assess the common region satisfying several linear inequalities. The supplied circle and line/curve-intersection teaching pages do not establish this method.
questions.methodNote: Provisional standard method: draw solid boundary lines for inclusive inequalities, identify their common half-planes and calculate boundary intersections. The original Chapter 11 inequality-region demonstrations were not supplied.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine several inclusive linear inequalities and calculate the vertices of their common region.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose the appropriate right-triangle ratio and invert or rearrange it; the hardest part first recognises the right triangle made by perpendicular rhombus diagonals. This is routine linked geometric and trigonometric reasoning for a prepared student.

questions.mappingNote: Part a uses inverse sine with opposite side and hypotenuse; part b uses tangent with adjacent side and opposite side; part c uses perpendicular rhombus diagonals followed by cosine with the unknown hypotenuse. The offered sine-rule reuse candidate has different givens, diagrams and assessed methods and is not source-equivalent.
questions.methodNote: The supplied original pages demonstrate forming a right triangle, using tangent and inverse tangent, rearranging a trigonometric ratio and retaining unrounded intermediate values. The initial teaching of sine, cosine and inverse sine is not supplied.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select right-triangle ratios, including recognising the right triangle formed by the diagonals of a rhombus.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the ladder as the hypotenuse and use cosine and sine with the angle measured from the vertical.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts assess practical right-triangle side calculations. The supplied example supports the method, although the original introductory sine and cosine teaching is not supplied.
questions.methodNote: The inspected Example 6 uses right-triangle trigonometric ratios to find practical distances and rounds only final results. Here cosine gives the vertical distance and sine gives the horizontal distance from the angle with the vertical.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the ladder as the hypotenuse and use cosine and sine with the angle measured from the vertical.

classification.difficultyReason: Represent the tree and shadow as a right triangle, convert their lengths to common units and select inverse tangent for the elevation angle.

questions.mappingNote: The tree height is opposite the elevation angle and the horizontal shadow is adjacent; convert both lengths to the same unit before applying inverse tangent.
questions.methodNote: The supplied original page 9 defines elevation from the horizontal and demonstrates tangent for an unknown angle. Page 10 demonstrates selecting the vertical right triangle and retaining unrounded values.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Represent the tree and shadow as a right triangle, convert their lengths to common units and select inverse tangent for the elevation angle.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine three compass-directed displacements, then use a right triangle to calculate distance and a reverse bearing.

questions.mappingNote: Part a uses the net perpendicular north–west displacements as the legs of a right triangle. Part b uses inverse tangent and the clockwise bearing convention at the final position.
questions.methodNote: The supplied original page 9 demonstrates Pythagoras’ theorem, inverse tangent and clockwise true bearings from north. Page 10 separates the relevant right triangles and retains unrounded intermediate values.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine three compass-directed displacements, then use a right triangle to calculate distance and a reverse bearing.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise perpendicular flight legs, calculate the resultant direction using a right triangle, then reverse the bearing.

questions.mappingNote: The two flight legs are perpendicular. An inverse tangent gives the angle between the first leg and the resultant displacement; the required direction is the reverse bearing.
questions.methodNote: The inspected originals define true bearings clockwise from north and demonstrate identifying a right triangle, applying a trigonometric ratio and retaining unrounded intermediate values.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise perpendicular flight legs, calculate the resultant direction using a right triangle, then reverse the bearing.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret the limiting line of sight over the dune and use the same angle in two right triangles.

questions.mappingNote: Use one sight-line angle in the right triangle from the shoreline to the dune crest and in the right triangle from the shoreline to the observer’s eye. The dune is 100 m from the sea; the observer is 350 m from the sea.
questions.methodNote: The supplied original pages define elevation and depression relative to the horizontal and demonstrate tangent as vertical height divided by horizontal distance. Keep the ratio exact until the final result.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret the limiting line of sight over the dune and use the same angle in two right triangles.

classification.difficultyReason: Bisect the isosceles triangle formed by two radii and the chord, then use right-triangle trigonometry to determine three related lengths.

questions.mappingNote: This is a practical right-triangle trigonometry problem requiring a geometric construction before calculation; exact ratios support retaining precision across dependent parts.
questions.methodNote: The inspected Chapter 19 page supplies exact 60-degree ratios and their right-triangle representations. The inspected Chapter 12 example demonstrates selecting right triangles and retaining unrounded intermediate values. Bisect the isosceles radius triangle, use tangent for the perpendicular distance and sine for the radius, then subtract exact lengths for the water depth.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Bisect the isosceles triangle formed by two radii and the chord, then use right-triangle trigonometry to determine three related lengths.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply exact ratios; the second part links two right triangles and requires solving an equation involving a surd.

questions.mappingNote: Part a directly uses an exact sine ratio. Part b applies exact tangent ratios to two linked right triangles, uses segment addition, and simplifies the resulting surd expression. The supplied sine-rule reuse candidate has different givens, diagrams and assessed tasks and is inapplicable.
questions.methodNote: The inspected exact-values table and right-triangle representations establish sin 30 degrees = 1/2, tan 45 degrees = 1 and tan 60 degrees = square root of 3. Apply these ratios without decimal approximations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply exact ratios; the second part links two right triangles and requires solving an equation involving a surd.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine exact tangent ratios in two right triangles using the total base length, then rationalise a binomial surd denominator.

questions.mappingNote: Chapter 19 page 6 supplies the exact ratios and their right-triangle representations. Chapter 12 page 9 demonstrates right-triangle tangent working. The supplied evidence does not include the original conjugate-rationalisation demonstration.
questions.methodNote: Use exact tangent ratios for 45 and 30 degrees in the two right triangles, express both horizontal lengths in terms of x, and use their sum of 100 cm. Rationalise the resulting denominator.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine exact tangent ratios in two right triangles using the total base length, then rationalise a binomial surd denominator.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine exact special-triangle side ratios with a perimeter equation and rationalise a binomial surd denominator.

questions.mappingNote: The inspected Chapter 19 page 6 supplies the exact ratios and special-triangle representation. Original conjugate-rationalisation teaching is absent from the supplied evidence.
questions.methodNote: Use the displayed exact 30°, 60° and 90° triangle ratios to express both shorter sides in terms of the hypotenuse, apply the perimeter, and rationalise the resulting denominator with its conjugate.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine exact special-triangle side ratios with a perimeter equation and rationalise a binomial surd denominator.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct the travel-and-lighthouse triangle from bearings, use a reverse bearing to obtain its angles and recognise equal opposite sides after calculating the travel distance.

questions.mappingNote: The inspected bearing definition establishes the direction convention. The inspected sine-rule teaching establishes opposite side–angle pairs for this non-right triangle. Its two 30-degree angles allow the final side equality directly.
questions.methodNote: Use clockwise true bearings to determine the triangle’s interior angles. Equal opposite angles give equal sides; the sine rule gives the same result.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct the travel-and-lighthouse triangle from bearings, use a reverse bearing to obtain its angles and recognise equal opposite sides after calculating the travel distance.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify opposite side–angle pairs, calculate missing angles and use the sine rule to complete three triangles.

questions.mappingNote: The inspected sine-rule derivation supports the side calculations and opposite-pair notation. The inspected worked example supports retaining calculator precision. Explicit inverse-sine and ambiguous-case teaching was not supplied.
questions.methodNote: Use opposite side–angle pairs in the sine rule and the triangle angle sum; retain unrounded intermediate values. Parts a and b each have only one geometrically possible inverse-sine result.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify opposite side–angle pairs, calculate missing angles and use the sine rule to complete three triangles.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert successive true bearings into the included triangle angle, then apply the cosine rule.

questions.mappingNote: The supplied Chapter 12 page 9 defines true bearings; page 25 states the cosine rule for two sides and the included angle. These directly support this two-leg journey calculation.
questions.methodNote: Use clockwise true bearings to determine the interior angle, then use the cosine rule with two sides and their included angle.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert successive true bearings into the included triangle angle, then apply the cosine rule.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine two right-triangle tangent relationships using the difference between the horizontal distances.

questions.mappingNote: External page 9 defines elevation; page 10 demonstrates tangent relating vertical height and horizontal distance and retaining unrounded intermediate values. The source diagram assigns 14 degrees to A and 43 degrees to B.
questions.methodNote: Use tangent in the two vertical right triangles, with angles of elevation measured from horizontal ground. Retain exact trigonometric expressions until the final rounding.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine two right-triangle tangent relationships using the difference between the horizontal distances.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret two bearings, construct related right triangles and solve simultaneous distance relationships using exact trigonometric ratios.

questions.mappingNote: Chapter 12 page 9 establishes the bearing convention, page 10 demonstrates separating right triangles, and Chapter 19 page 6 supplies exact 45° and 60° ratios. Chapter2 source18 printed56 explicitly derives conjugate rationalisation using the difference-of-squares identity; supplied original pixels permit independent compatibility review.
questions.methodNote: Measure true bearings clockwise from north; resolve the configuration into right triangles and use exact tangent and cosine ratios. Solve the resulting linear equation and rationalise its surd denominator.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret two bearings, construct related right triangles and solve simultaneous distance relationships using exact trigonometric ratios.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the perpendicular projection onto each of two different planes, calculate a face diagonal and use trigonometry to find each inclination.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly assess angles between a line and a plane. Part a uses base diagonal AC and triangle ACG; part b uses side-face diagonal BG and triangle BGH. The solutions explain the required projections, but their compatibility with the original inclination demonstration remains unverified. Explicit user source decision on 23 October 2026: "Keep the original assumed knowledge". Retain the original assumed inclination conventions. Do not add the proposed definitions or infer that an original page contains them. This source decision is not mathematical/content acceptance; independently verify the unchanged original task, diagram and all answers.
questions.methodNote: The supplied Chapter 12 pages demonstrate face-diagonal Pythagoras followed by right-triangle trigonometry, separation of relevant triangles, and retention of unrounded intermediate values. Explicit teaching of inclination through perpendicular projection is absent.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the perpendicular projection onto each of two different planes, calculate a face diagonal and use trigonometry to find each inclination.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish a face–base angle from an edge–base angle and use two different vertical sections of a square pyramid.

questions.mappingNote: The supplied Chapter 12 pages demonstrate right-triangle calculations and separating horizontal and vertical triangles; page 11 supplies square-pyramid practice context. Chapter 19 page 6 supplies the exact 60-degree ratio. Explicit teaching of face–base and edge–base inclination constructions is absent, so compatibility of those constructions remains unresolved. Explicit user source decision on 23 October 2026: "Keep the original assumed knowledge". Retain the original assumed inclination conventions. Do not add the proposed definitions or infer that an original page contains them. This source decision is not mathematical/content acceptance; independently verify the unchanged original task, diagram and all answers.
questions.methodNote: Use the vertical section through the apex, base centre and midpoint of a base side for the face–base angle. Use the section through the apex, base centre and a base vertex for the edge–base angle and edge length. Apply tangent, exact ratios and Pythagoras, retaining exact intermediate lengths.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Distinguish a face–base angle from an edge–base angle and use two different vertical sections of a square pyramid.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the perpendicular projection of a space diagonal onto a face, then calculate its inclination.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed angle is between CE and its projection AE in the specified face; use Pythagoras before a tangent ratio.
questions.methodNote: The inspected worked example separates horizontal and vertical right triangles and retains exact intermediate values. The inspected practice page includes angles involving inclined planes. Explicit line-to-plane projection teaching is not supplied.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the perpendicular projection of a space diagonal onto a face, then calculate its inclination.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish a face inclination from a rafter inclination using the roof's plan and vertical rise.

questions.mappingNote: Part a uses a section perpendicular to BC; part b uses the rafter's horizontal projection.
questions.methodNote: Separate horizontal and vertical right triangles and keep intermediate lengths exact. Explicit teaching of the perpendicular cross-section defining a face inclination is missing.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Distinguish a face inclination from a rafter inclination using the roof's plan and vertical rise.

classification.difficultyReason: Without intermediate scaffolding, identify and justify where a moving point gives the least and greatest spatial angle, then construct suitable right triangles to calculate both extrema.

questions.mappingNote: At an endpoint use a right triangle; at the midpoint bisect the isosceles triangle. Numerical results and locations agree with the teacher answer.
questions.methodNote: The inspected evidence supports cube face diagonals, right-triangle trigonometry and retaining exact intermediate lengths. A taught geometric justification for the variable-point extrema is not supplied.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Without intermediate scaffolding, identify and justify where a moving point gives the least and greatest spatial angle, then construct suitable right triangles to calculate both extrema.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine semicircle and centre–circumference angle properties with an equilateral triangle, then use Pythagoras to find an exact length.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a(i), a(iii) and a(iv) directly assess circle angle properties; a(ii) establishes the central angle using an equilateral triangle. Part b combines the semicircle result with finding a shorter side by Pythagoras. The boxed theorem on the teaching page supplies the correct centre-to-circumference relationship; its example’s reversed explanatory wording is not reproduced.
questions.methodNote: The supplied Chapter 13 page 5 teaches the semicircle case and the centre–circumference theorem. Equal radii and the given BC=OB make BOC equilateral; the right triangle ABC then permits Pythagoras with exact surd arithmetic.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine semicircle and centre–circumference angle properties with an equilateral triangle, then use Pythagoras to find an exact length.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine equal tangents, an isosceles right triangle and the radius–tangent relationship to prove an angle bisector.

questions.mappingNote: The supplied external original page 25 contains tangent and radius reasoning and equal-tangent deductions. These support the proof directly; no product-rule or alternate-segment method is required.
questions.methodNote: Use equality of tangents from an external point, equal base angles in an isosceles triangle, the triangle angle sum, and perpendicularity of a tangent and radius at contact.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine equal tangents, an isosceles right triangle and the radius–tangent relationship to prove an angle bisector.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the intersecting-chords product rule directly to three supplied segment lengths and divide to obtain the fourth.

questions.mappingNote: AE and EC are the intercepts on one chord; BE and DE are the intercepts on the other. The question directly assesses the intersecting-chords product rule.
questions.methodNote: Chapter 13 PDF page 31 states and proves the intersecting-chords equal-products rule. Page 32 Example 9(a) substitutes the given intercept lengths and solves for the remaining length.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the intersecting-chords product rule directly to three supplied segment lengths and divide to obtain the fourth.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the external-secant product rule, distinguishing whole secant lengths from their internal portions.

questions.mappingNote: Question 5 directly assesses this theorem: RP=RQ+QP and RT=RS+ST. The supplied reuse candidates do not contain this original task.
questions.methodNote: The external-secant theorem equates products of lengths measured from the external point. Example 9(b) forms each whole secant by adding its external and internal portions before solving.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the external-secant product rule, distinguishing whole secant lengths from their internal portions.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise similar triangles using exterior angles of a cyclic quadrilateral, then use corresponding sides to find two lengths.

questions.mappingNote: The extended sides form triangles EAD and ECB. Their corresponding sides AD and CB give the scale ratio needed for both requested lengths.
questions.methodNote: Use supplementary opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral to establish exterior-angle equalities, prove triangle similarity, and equate corresponding side ratios.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise similar triangles using exterior angles of a cyclic quadrilateral, then use corresponding sides to find two lengths.

classification.difficultyReason: Discover an unsignposted SAS similarity from the product equality, transfer its angle relationship to a second triangle pair and convert that similarity into the required product.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed task is a two-stage similarity proof; no converse intersecting-chords theorem is assumed.
questions.methodNote: Use proportional sides and vertically opposite angles to establish SAS similarity, then corresponding angles to establish a second similarity and equate matching side ratios. The supplied circle proofs also use triangle similarity followed by matching-side ratios and a product equality.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Discover an unsignposted SAS similarity from the product equality, transfer its angle relationship to a second triangle pair and convert that similarity into the required product.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the tangent–secant product rule, express the whole secant using its two segments, and reject a negative length when solving the quadratic in part c.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts directly assess the tangent–secant product rule. Part c additionally requires factorising a quadratic and selecting the positive length.
questions.methodNote: The inspected original Chapter 13 page 32 states and proves that the product of the two secant intercepts measured from the external point equals the square of the tangent length. Its worked secant example adds the external and internal segments before applying the product rule.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the tangent–secant product rule, express the whole secant using its two segments, and reject a negative length when solving the quadratic in part c.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine the perpendicular radius–tangent relationship with equal base angles in an isosceles triangle.

questions.mappingNote: The tangent angle gives a base angle of triangle OBC; equal radii give the other base angle, determining the central angle.
questions.methodNote: Use the perpendicular radius–tangent relationship, equal radii and the angle sum of a triangle.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine the perpendicular radius–tangent relationship with equal base angles in an isosceles triangle.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine angle bisectors with the alternate segment theorem, then use supplementary angles and the converse of Thales’ theorem.

questions.mappingNote: Part a directly assesses the alternate segment theorem. Part b combines the given angle bisectors with the right-angle criterion for a diameter.
questions.methodNote: Use the alternate segment theorem to prove equal base angles for part a. For part b, halve supplementary angles and apply the converse of Thales’ theorem.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate logarithms by recognising positive integer powers, including the zero power.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c and e directly assess numerical logarithm evaluation using known integer powers; part d assesses the zero-power result. The supplied reuse candidates describe different complete tasks and are not source-equivalent.
questions.methodNote: Use the logarithm definition and Example 2 Method 1: express the argument as a power of the base, then read off the exponent. The standard result log_a 1=0 also supports part d.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate logarithms by recognising positive integer powers, including the zero power.

classification.difficultyReason: Express each argument as a negative integer power of its logarithm base.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts evaluate numerical logarithms of reciprocal powers or terminating decimals; no change of base or equation-solving method is required.
questions.methodNote: Rewrite the argument as a power of the base and use the logarithm definition. Example 2, Method 1, demonstrates negative-power evaluation of reciprocal arguments.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express each argument as a negative integer power of its logarithm base.

classification.difficultyReason: Select the product or quotient logarithm law from the displayed operation, then recognise a base or reciprocal-base argument when evaluation is possible.

questions.mappingNote: All nine parts assess simplifying logarithmic expressions; f–i additionally evaluate the resulting logarithm. The supplied reuse candidates have different original tasks and are inapplicable.
